text: Τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ. Accepit Maximus quo pacto Vulg. et reliqui fere interpretes, de ipso ejus filio, nempe regis Moab; qui ferali ea victima litandum Deo, dum extreme laborat, putaverit: forte etiam Abrahami exemplo, qui filii immolatione tentata, etsi non peracta, tantopere Deo placuerit: quod ita sensit R. Sal. Peræque tamen Græca vox αὐτοῦ, suum reddatur, referendo ad regem Moab, et ejus, referendo ad regem Edom, in quem facta irruptione rex Moab cum septingentis delectis suis, ad ipsum quidem non pervenerit, ejus tamen primogenitum ceperit, sicque super muros jugulaverit et incenderit; vel cum jam eum in captivis haberet; cujus etiam liberandi causa pater sociale bellum cum regibus Juda et Israel inierit: ejusque dissolvendæ societatis, ipsa hæc dira cædes et immanitas illi causa exstiterit, conversa ejus facinoris invidia in eos, qui belli auctores exstitissent, et ad eas angustias regem Moab redegissent. Hebr. perinde ambigua [Hebrew: את־בנו] filium suum, vel ejus: quo altero modo Pagn., Malvend., Munster, etc., interpretati sunt. Sic etiam qui Am. II, 1, incensa Idumææ regis ossa usque ad cineres, cujus rei causa sic Deus Moabitis comminatur, de hac cæde et holocausto exponunt; quorum sententiam parum pulsant rationes Santii, inque illis hæc potissima, quod rex dicatur illo Anios, cum IV Regum primogenitus regis solum appelletur, quod ad regis titulum non sufficit, ac nisi pater jam in eum jura regni transtulerat. Nam et hoc intellexerunt οἱ LXX, ὃς ἐβασίλευσε, quibus reddiderunt, ὃν ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ' αὐτοῦ, quem sui loco regem constituerat; vel, ut codex Alex. ὃς ἐβασίλευσε, qui ipse regnum capessiverat. Proinde quod Hebr. futuri temporis est, pro præterito positum intellexere. Quod item de ossibus ad cineres usque combustis exaggerat propheta, haud necesse trahere ad ossa e sepulcro effossa, cum nihil occurrat in Scriptura, quo referri possit ea tumuli ossiumque violatio; sed potest intelligi, sic in cineres et favillam redactum hujus principis corpus, relato de eo holocausto, ut nec ossa superfuerint, uti se fere habebant Romanorum ac gentium aliarum busta. In hac itaque satis probabili expositione non satis faveat istud exemplum Maximi scopo; velut scilicet divino instinctu, ad præfigurandum Christi mysterium, quasi piaculari hostia, sic captum hostem rex Moab holocausto obtulerit, eaque victima a se iram depulerit: quomodo etiamnum barbari Canadenses et alii hostes immolant, eorumque laute carnibus epulantur, nullo certe divino instinctu, quo sic mala depellenda intelligant, sed ferina immanitate, ac diabolo instigante, qui sic humano delectetur cruore, Deumque olim æmuletur, nec ignobiliori quam humana sibi hostia, quibus impetrare possit, fieri velit. Christi sacrificium varie Deus in animalium victimis adumbravit; in hominum, nunquam, præterquam in uno Abrahamo et Isaaco, ad usque duntaxat propositi animi manifestationem. Et in ipso Christo victima fuit, quod se ipse obtulit, Judæorum malitia utens, nec tormenta abnuens, ut divinæ satis justitiæ fieret, non velut ipse seipsum interficiens, quod fecere gentilium quidam, nihil prorsus affini Christo exemplo, sed diabolico plane commento.
anchorLine: ὁ τῆς χώρας βασιλεὺς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ (l), κατ' ὀφθαλ-
en: On 'his son.' Maximus has taken it, as the Vulgate and nearly all other interpreters do, of his own son, namely the king of Moab's: he thought that in his extremity he must placate God with this deadly victim, perhaps also following the example of Abraham, who pleased God so greatly by the attempted, though uncompleted, sacrifice of his son; so R. Sal. understood it. Yet the Greek word autou may be rendered 'his own,' referring to the king of Moab, or 'of him,' referring to the king of Edom: against whom the king of Moab made a sortie with seven hundred picked men, did not reach him, but captured his firstborn and killed and burned him on the walls; or [it means] when he already had him among his captives, for whose release the father had begun a joint war with the kings of Judah and Israel, and this dreadful slaughter and cruelty became the cause of dissolving the alliance, the hatred of the deed turning on those who had been the authors of the war and had driven the king of Moab into such straits. The Hebrew is likewise ambiguous, 'his son' or 'of him'; Pagninus, Malvenda, Munster and others have interpreted it the second way. So too those who explain Amos 2:1 (the bones of the king of Edom burned to ashes, for which cause God so threatens the Moabites) of this slaughter and burnt offering; the arguments of Sanctius scarcely overthrow their view, chiefly that the man is called king in Amos, while 4 Kings calls him only the king's firstborn, which does not suffice for the title of king unless the father had already transferred the rights of the kingdom to him. For the Septuagint also understood this, 'who reigned,' which they rendered 'whom he had made king in his place'; or, as Codex Alexandrinus has it, 'who himself had taken the kingdom.' Hence they understood the Hebrew future as put for the past. As for the bones burned to ashes which the prophet exaggerates, there is no need to draw this to bones dug up from a tomb, since nothing in Scripture suggests such a violation of tomb and bones; it can rather be understood that this prince's body, once the burnt offering was made of him, was reduced to ashes and cinders so that not even bones remained, as the burial pyres of the Romans and other nations generally were. In this fairly probable explanation, the example does not much favour Maximus's aim: namely that, as by divine instinct to prefigure the mystery of Christ, the king of Moab offered the captured enemy as a burnt offering, like an expiatory victim, and so turned wrath from himself; just as barbarous Canadians and other peoples still sacrifice enemies and feast richly on their flesh, certainly with no divine instinct by which they might suppose evils are to be averted, but from savage cruelty, at the devil's instigation, who delights in human blood and once vied with God, and would not have them offer him a lesser victim than a human one by which they might obtain what they seek. God foreshadowed Christ's sacrifice in various ways in animal victims; in men never, save only in Abraham and Isaac, and then only up to the manifestation of the intention. And in Christ himself there was a victim, in that he offered himself, using the malice of the Jews and not refusing torments, so that divine justice might be satisfied, and not as one killing himself, as some of the heathen did -- an example wholly unlike Christ, and plainly a diabolical invention.

text: Πρὸς Κυρισίκιον. Haud a mendo abesse videtur, quod ita prænotatur. Ac num πρὸς Κυζικινόν, ad Joannem scilicet Cyzicenum episcopum, ad quem ipsum abhinc secunda et tertia, affini plane argumento; etsi ibi sedis locus tacetur, nec nisi ad Joannem episcopum dicitur; vel num hæc et sequens ad Constantinopolitanum ipsum episcopum, a quo ad se revocari petat, si modo timor abscesserit hostium? Alias et alias subinde Maximus videtur mutasse sedes, nedum cum in Africam commeavit, Persarum metu, verum etiam aliis occasionibus, quo factum est, ut sit obscurum, cujus potissimum episcopi conspectibus aliis aliisque epistolis petat restitui. Omnes tamen hæ quinque ad eumdem videntur spectare, ex ipsa argumenti affinitate; exque Georgii abbatis et presbyteri secunda et quarta mentione, conjectura firmatur, eumdem ipsum Joannem episcopum Cyzicenum Maximo amicissimum, probeque orthodoxum, illis omnibus compellari, quod præcipue non sic ei cum sede Constantinopolitana conveniebat, cum hæc [?]iberet, et jam depulsus Persarum timor videre[tur?]
anchorLine: ΚΙΙ'. — Τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς Κυρισίκιον (m) ἐπίσκοπον.
en: To Cyrisicius. This heading seems not to be free of error, as it is entitled. Might it be 'to Cyzicinus,' that is, to John, bishop of Cyzicus, to whom the next second and third letters are addressed, with a plainly similar subject; although there the place of his see is not mentioned and he is addressed only as John the bishop? Or are this letter and the following addressed to the bishop of Constantinople himself, from whom he asks to be recalled to him, if only the fear of enemies has gone? Maximus seems to have changed his residence again and again, not only when he went to Africa for fear of the Persians but also on other occasions, so that it is unclear to which bishop's presence he asks, in one letter and another, to be restored. Yet all these five seem to be directed to the same man, from the similarity of subject; and from the second and fourth mention of Georgius the abbot and presbyter it is confirmed by conjecture that the same John, bishop of Cyzicus, a very close friend of Maximus and thoroughly orthodox, is addressed in all of them, since he was not on such terms with the see of Constantinople, when this [text lost in the damaged line] and now the fear of the Persians, driven off, seemed [text breaks off; continuation on the next page].

text: [videre]tur, Pyrrho forsitan jam episcopo, vel etiam intruso Paulo, per cujus intrusi grassationem Pyrrhus Maximum convenit in Africa, quocum disputans, errorem agnovit. Non tamen de ejus tropæo loqui videtur, cum altera hinc epistola gregi sic peregre profecto, et qui ingentia maris spatia trajecerat, gratuletur, quod λύκων ἀναιρετική exstiterit. Lupos peremerit; Severianos potius significet, de quibus majori epistola ad Joann. cubicularium, vel etiam Monothelitas in Africa per fugæ ab urbe et patria occasionem, hæresis semina spargentes, quibus comprimendis celebratæ Africæ synodi Theodoro Romano pontifice: qua in re, non unius Maximi, sed reliquorum sodalium monachorum, qui vere orthodoxi essent, enituerit opera
en: [Continuation of the note (m) from p. 344: ...it seemed that the fear of the Persians had been driven off] perhaps to Pyrrhus, already bishop, or even to the intruder Paul, through whose intruding aggression Pyrrhus met Maximus in Africa and, disputing with him, acknowledged his error. Yet he does not seem to speak of his triumph, since another letter here congratulates the flock that has gone abroad, and which had crossed the vast spaces of the sea, that it proved a 'destroyer of wolves.' He may mean he has slain wolves, the Severians rather, of whom [there is mention] in the longer letter to John the chamberlain; or even the Monothelites in Africa who, taking the occasion of flight from city and homeland, scatter the seeds of heresy; in suppressing whom, at the synods of Africa held under Pope Theodore of Rome, the work shone out not of Maximus alone but of the rest of his fellow monks who were truly orthodox [text breaks off, no full stop].

text: Περὶ θετικῆς. Imposuerat istud tituli, cum a viro doctissimo abbate Bigotio Florentia accepissem, nec ille aliud quam titulum raptim legisset. Nactus vero ejus opera cam epistolam, omnem excussi scrupulum; mendo ipso clare deprehenso, ac legendum παραθετική, hoc est, συστατική, Commendatitia scilicet epistola, pro Georgio Africæ præfecto, cum is incerto eventu Constantinopolim evocatus esset. Joannes cubicularius, quasi scilicet sacri cubiculi præfectus, magnæ auctoritatis in aula erat, idem Maximi perquam amicus, ad quem ille pleraque et propria et communia referebat. Quæ sequitur, ipsa ejusdem argumenti est, mirasque ambæ Georgii laudes continent, quas Maximus æmulorum calumniis opponit: quibus tandem vir tantus oppressus, defectionem fecit, dataque semel Vandalis occasione, ab eis Africam liberare non potuit.
anchorLine: περὶ θετικῆς (n).
en: On 'Peri thetikes.' I had put this down as the title when I received it from the very learned abbot Bigot at Florence, and he had himself read nothing but the title in haste. Having got the letter itself through his work, I removed every doubt: the error was plainly detected, and one must read paratheitke, that is sustatike, a commendatory letter, for George, prefect of Africa, when he had been summoned to Constantinople with an uncertain outcome. John the chamberlain, as being prefect of the sacred bedchamber, was a man of great authority at court, and a very close friend of Maximus, to whom Maximus reported most of his private and common affairs. The letter that follows is of the same subject, and both contain wonderful praises of George, which Maximus sets against the slanders of his rivals; by whom at length so great a man was overwhelmed, made his revolt, and, once he had given the Vandals the opportunity, could not free Africa from them.
